title: Every requirement raised for this system, where it came from, and whether it holds
summary:
One hundred and one requirements — functional and non-functional — mined from nine commits, the 88 gap entries on the six pages beside this one, the migrations that are the real contract, and three external findings that never touched the code. Each carries an origin, a status verified against this tree rather than copied from the commit that claimed it, and the command that decided it.

Read it for three things the area pages cannot show. The couplings: one guard in `runNode` is the sole blocker under four separate requirements, which makes `OPS-04` the cheapest fix in the register and the one that unblocks the most. The wrong remedies: three surfaces tell an operator that something is protected when it is not — the printed auth fix, the revoke response's host proxy, and a reset step that reports `ok` while cleaning nothing — and a wrong remedy is worse than a documented absence. And the requirements with no code at all: managed device clouds are excluded by four suppliers' contracts, and the fire mitigation this rack needs turns out to be a `dumpsys battery` call that nobody has written.

sections.heading: Why this page exists, and what a status means on it
sections.body:
A requirement and a gap are the same object seen from two sides. The six pages beside this one document 88 gaps precisely and never say what any of them was supposed to be doing. `The fence is not enforced at the resource` is only legible next to `a fenced holder must not be able to reach the device`.

So this page is the other side: every requirement this system has been given, functional and non-functional, with where it came from, whether it holds today, and the check that decided it. Statuses were verified against the code, not copied from the commit that claimed them — several rows below disagree with the message that raised them.

Two structural facts several rows depend on. **The demo is not the system**: `internal/demo` writes `farm.device_runtime`, `farm.recovery_attempts`, `farm.quarantines`, `farm.events` and `farm.jobs.state` with its own rules, so a row it wrote proves the schema works and proves nothing about the loop whose job it is. And **nothing runs as its own Postgres role**: `farm_reaper`, `farm_scheduler` and `farm_watchdog` are created `NOLOGIN` and every process connects with one `DATABASE_URL`.
bullets: **Origins** are cited as `c:<sha>` for a commit, `gap:<area>.<n>` for entry *n* of that area page's `gaps` array, `schema` when the migration is the contract, `cap:features` for an entry in `featureStatuses()`, and `research:*` for an external finding.
An ID names where a requirement **lives**, not where it is violated: the fence-at-the-resource requirement is `SEC-04` even though its absence is felt in the lease protocol.
The full register, with the long-form evidence for every row, is `REQUIREMENTS.md` at the repository root. This page is that file rendered where an operator already is.

rows: Implemented, and demonstrated to work. The only status that means stop reading.
Implemented, with a named hole. The row names it.
Nothing in the tree implements it.
Implemented, reachable only on Linux — and not reachable in any deployment that ships today.
Implemented and plausibly correct, never observed working.
Raised, answered by a decision rather than by code. No implementation is owed.

sections.heading: The founding requirement
sections.body:
One requirement produced this system, and it came from somebody else's incident: DeviceFarmer/STF issue #663, open and unanswered since 2023. A device running automation gets an `ECONNRESET` after about ninety minutes and is automatically released mid-run, destroying hours of work.

The requirement is not `handle transport failures gracefully`. It is that the failure must be **unrepresentable**. A lease ends when the job says so, when a written-down deadline elapses, or when a human takes it back — and there is no fourth way to write it down.

examples.label: The requirement, as a CHECK constraint
examples.note: Seven values, none of them connectivity-flavoured. `released because the transport dropped` cannot be spelled. This is LEASE-01, and it is the one requirement in the register that is enforced in four independent places rather than one.

sections.heading: LEASE — the lease protocol
sections.body: Fourteen requirements: the invariant itself and everything that protects it. Six hold outright. The interesting failures are not the missing features — they are the two places where a protection exists in DDL that no deployment assumes (`LEASE-03`), and where a second automatic ending exists that none of the reaper's controls reach (`LEASE-08`).

rows: A lease ends when the job says so, when a written-down deadline elapses, or when a human takes it back. Never because of connectivity.
`farm.leases.release_reason` is CHECK-constrained to seven values with no connectivity term. Unrepresentable, not handled.
Lease liveness, job liveness and device health are three clocks, separated by table, by function and by Postgres role.
Distinct tables with distinct writers; `internal/watchdog` has no lease write path; `obs.TransportBlip` takes no lease identifier and returns nothing, so transport code has no value to branch on.
Reclamation must be structurally unable to read device health.

The DDL is right — function-level `SET role = farm_reaper` plus a revoked SELECT. Nothing assumes it: no Go code issues `SET ROLE`, the roles are `NOLOGIN`, the demo connects as a superuser. What actually holds is the Go import barrier. `gap:lease.10`
The witness cap counts only **consecutive** witness-only extensions, so a renew resets it.
`migrations/00002_lease.sql:328`. Without it a job expires 12 minutes into any run that witnesses once.
A control-plane outage is refunded to the tenant, computed across every component on the renewal path.

Correct for the components it is given. `jobrunner` beats and is not watched; a watched component that never beat contributes nothing to the `min()` rather than reading as infinitely stale; `FARM_COMPONENT` is honoured only by `api`. `gap:operate.5`, `gap:operate.6`, `gap:operate.7`
Every mutating lease function matches on `(id, fence)`, so a stale holder's write is rejected in the database.
`test/assertions.sql` proves the pod-eviction re-attach at an unchanged fence.
A zero-row renew (fenced, terminal) must never be conflated with a transient database error (retry).

`internal/lease/holder.go` splits `ErrFenced` from transient; the API splits 410 from 503. The branch its own comment calls the single most consequential decision in the project has no test — `leaseOps` exists so a stub could drive it and nothing does. `gap:lease.6`
The `max_runtime` sweep must fence the ended holder and rearm its slot, as release and reclaim do.

`farm.lease_expire_max_runtime` bumps neither `fence_floor` nor `slots.rearm_at`, has no `protected` filter, and is gated by neither `reaper_state.enabled` nor `quiesce_until`. Verified: after a sweep the ended holder's write at the same fence was **accepted**.
A job demonstrably alive on the device but blind to the control plane can extend its lease.

`farm.lease_witness`, `Store.Witness`, `Holder.Witness` and two config variables all exist. `Holder.Witness` has one caller and it is inside `internal/lease`. Across 1117 leases, `witness_at` is NULL on every one.
A protected lease is never auto-reclaimed; it is held and a human is paged.

The behaviour is correct. Its regression test is not watching it: P10 cannot move `expires_at` backwards, so both functions match zero rows and the assertion passes trivially. And nobody is paged — see `OBS-08`.
The automatic release path has an operator-reachable kill switch.

`farm.reaper_state.enabled` is read on every `lease_reclaim` and written by no route, no `ctl` command and no dashboard control. Turning the reaper off is a hand-written UPDATE with no audit row — and it does not stop `max_runtime`.

`jobrunner.Config` is built with no `HolderConfig`, so every holder uses `DefaultRenewInterval` (60s). The startup assertion guaranteeing three renewals inside the TTL guards a value no holder reads; the value they do read satisfies it by coincidence.
`FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS` cannot be set to something that fuses the health clock into the lease clock.

The config refuses to omit a renewal-path component and never refuses to add one. Adding `watchdog` makes a health-plane outage extend every lease in the farm. Prohibited in two doc comments, enforced nowhere.
The way a lease ended is recoverable from an event log at 3am.

1239 leases with `released_at` set; 0 `lease_released` events, 0 `lease_reclaimed`, 1 `lease_revoked`. The sweep writes no event. The authoritative record is `farm.leases.state` plus `release_reason`; `farm.events` is commentary.

sections.heading: DEV — device identity, topology and health
sections.body:
Twelve requirements. The identity model is the strongest thing in the system and the enrollment loop that would exercise it has never run, anywhere, for a reason that is one guard in `runNode` (`OPS-04`).

`DEV-09` is the sharpest row in the register: a fleet whose fire mitigation is charge limiting and early thermal detection (`HW-03`) has a schema column for each and collects neither.

rows: Every call that targets a physical position is addressed by USB devpath, never by serial.

`internal/adbwire` has zero internal dependencies and a test that fails the build if allocation vocabulary appears in it — it caught a comment its own author wrote. A clone test asserts a devpath-addressed command reaches exactly one of two devices sharing `0123456789ABCDEF`.
One function owns `is this the device we think it is`, resolving strongest evidence first.

The ladder is right; two rungs do not work. Rung 2 calls `min()` on a `uuid` and PostgreSQL 17 has no such aggregate, so the sighting parks at `pending` forever. Rung 3 sets `ambiguous` but leaves the device NULL and rung 4 tests only for NULL, so a clone in an empty slot is adopted as new. `gap:devices.0`, `gap:devices.1`
A device sharing a serial with another is flagged durably, not just logged.

`serial_ambiguous` is written only from inside `farm.resolve_device`. The watchdog and enroller only log. On any farm where enrollment is not running — every farm today — a new clone pair produces a log line and no durable flag.
A handset plugged into a host joins the fleet without a human writing SQL.
`enroll.New` has exactly one construction site, inside `runNode`, and `farmd node` cannot start. No process anywhere calls `farm.resolve_device`. The capability panel above reports this honestly.
A host reports its USB tree and the controller, hub, power domain and slot rows grow to fit.

`farm.register_slot` works and was verified directly. `internal/topo/sysfs.go` refuses off Linux, and the only role that would call it cannot start. `farm.slot_occupancy` has 0 rows and all 56 devices have `hw_fingerprint IS NULL`.
A hub without per-port switching gets ONE ganged power domain, so the ladder cannot cycle seven devices to fix one.

The model is right. The demo seed gives every hub one domain including hubs whose kind is `per_port`, so tier 4's blast radius is the whole hub on hardware that could switch one port. `gap:recovery.15`
A slot is marked, never deleted, and a hub that vanishes is reconciled.

Marking works; reconciliation is off everywhere. `topo.Config`'s `RetireVanished`, `Overrides`, `AdoptEmpty`, `MinPorts`, `DryRun` and `MaxRetireFraction` are wired to no config field or flag. A hub you unplug leaves its slots `active` forever.
An operator can register a slot, re-slot a device or rebrand one without hand-written SQL.

`farm.register_slot` is SQL-only; `enroll.Brander.Rebrand` has no callers. The brand-conflict error tells the operator a human must retire one of the rows and gives them no command with which to do it.
Battery state of charge, battery temperature and the charge gate are collected per device.

The columns exist, `farm.v_fleet` exposes them, the API serialises them and `ctl` prints them. The only writer in the tree is `internal/demo/seed.go`, once, at seed time. No code runs `dumpsys battery`.
Health is a token bucket, not a raw counter, so a device cannot flap on every blip.

The damper is implemented and asymmetric by design. On the demo `farm.device_runtime` has two writers with different rules, and the simulator ignores `suppress_until` entirely — so every `degraded` row you can see here came from the simulator. `gap:devices.9`
The ADB host protocol and the sync protocol are spoken natively, with no shelling out to `adb`.

Both implemented; the sync work found the per-transfer context was decorative, so against a silent device a step's timeout could never fire. SEND, RECV, LSTAT_V1 and QUIT only: no enumeration, no mkdir, and `FileInfo.Size` truncates from a `uint32` above 4 GiB. `gap:devices.12`
The health plane can never touch a lease.
`REVOKE ALL ON farm.leases FROM farm_watchdog` plus the Go import barrier. See `LEASE-03` for why the first half binds nothing at runtime; the second half holds.

examples.label: DEV-09: every mention of battery telemetry in the tree
examples.output:
./internal/api/fleet.go:31:  f.adb_state, f.health, f.health_since, f.battery_pct::int, f.battery_temp_dc::int,
./internal/api/fleet.go:73:	BatteryPct      *int       `json:"battery_pct,omitempty"`
./internal/ctl/commands.go:77:	BatteryPct      *int       `json:"battery_pct"`
./internal/demo/seed.go:358:                                 battery_pct, battery_temp_dc, charge_gate, boot_completed,
./migrations/00001_core.sql:209:  battery_pct   smallint CHECK (battery_pct BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
./migrations/00003_ops.sql:204:       r.battery_pct,
examples.note: A schema column, a view, an API field and a CLI column — and exactly one writer, `internal/demo/seed.go`, which runs once at seed time. `battery_temp_dc` and `charge_gate` have the same shape. The plumbing for a physical safety control is complete except for the `dumpsys battery` call at the end of it.

sections.heading: JOB — the step model, execution and configuration
sections.body:
Twelve requirements. `JOB-02` is the thesis of the project and it works, observed repeatedly. Most of the rest describe a job that can be filed but not configured, not validated, and not read back afterwards.

The pattern worth naming: three separate rows (`JOB-05`, `JOB-06`, `JOB-11`) are cases where the mechanism is fully written and the one call site or one column write that would activate it is missing. None is a design problem.

rows: The step vocabulary is closed and the database owns it, so a spec written today means the same thing when it resumes tomorrow.
`farm.step_kinds` carries the ten kinds and the idempotent flag a resume needs. `TestKindTableMatchesMigration` pins the Go vocabulary to the migration and fails if they drift.
A transport failure inside a step is retried inside the lease, bounded only by a deadline the job's author wrote down.

Observed: a job survived 8 ADB transport blips across 4 renewals and completed all 10 steps; a later run survived six failures inside the lease that held them. This is the requirement the project is named for and it is the one that works.
Long work runs detached on the device so no socket is the source of truth.

Implemented; the demo's own soak was rewritten from 2000 ADB round trips into one detached command plus a poll. The exit code is never read: a detached command that exited 137 produces a green step and a green `wait_for`. `gap:jobs.10`
A job checkpoints and resumes, re-running nothing whose side effect would repeat.

The code and the idempotent flag it keys on are both there. The demo has never exercised resume. `runner.Conn` is documented as an interface specifically so `planResume` could be driven by a fake; that fake does not exist. `gap:jobs.7`
A spec is validated before a device is allocated to it.

`specSubmissionError` exists, is documented as the gate, and is called from nowhere. Verified live: seven jobs failed with `jobspec: invalid spec`, each having burned an attempt on a **different** real device.
A reset tier expands into a real step list from the job's profile, so reset is generic.

The expansion works and `GET /api/v1/specs/resets` shows it. `farm.jobs.profile_id` is never written — two hits in the tree, both reads. Every reset above `none` expands to zero sub-steps, reports `ok`, and cleans nothing. `gap:jobs.2`
The per-job knobs the runner reads are settable when the job is filed.

`profile_id`, `reset_tier`, `max_attempts` and `resumable` are all in `farm.jobs` and none is in `jobCreateRequest` or any `ctl` flag. A job that must never be retried on a second device can only be configured by an UPDATE between the insert and the placement.
An operator can see which step failed, and what it printed, without a database session.

`farm.job_steps` and `farm.job_attempts` have no route. `GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}` returns two keys. `ctl job` prints the spec and the lease history. The SSE digest carries five fields, none of them a step.
A step or attempt row whose process died is closed by something.

`internal/runner` is the only writer and there is no sweeper. The `job_steps_live` partial index exists and no query uses it. Verified: a `succeeded` job with an attempt open 19 minutes at NULL outcome and a step still `running`.
A job's reported state agrees with its step rows.

It does not. Reproduced twice: an `install` whose push failed left step 1 `running`, step 2 never created, the job `succeeded` and the lease released `completed`. `farm.device_artifacts` is the only place the truth survives.
`farm.jobs.selector` is stored, validated and echoed. The string `selector` does not occur anywhere in `migrations/00002_lease.sql`. Only `pin_device` narrows placement.
A payload cannot lie about its kind, and an unrunnable spec cannot be accepted unchecked.

Found by running it: both `Shell` and `*Shell` satisfied `Payload` because `Kind()` has a value receiver, and the pointer form **skipped every validation rule**. Both paths now normalise, with a regression test that fails if the rules stop firing.

examples.label: JOB-05: the gate, and its call sites
examples.output:
./internal/api/specs.go:565:// specSubmissionError is the gate POST /api/v1/jobs applies to a spec.
./internal/api/specs.go:576:func specSubmissionError(raw json.RawMessage) *APIError {
examples.note: Two hits: the doc comment describing it as a gate, and the definition. Nothing calls it. `handleJobCreate` inserts the spec straight into `farm.jobs`, so the first thing that reads it is `jobspec.Parse` inside the runner — after the scheduler has taken a phone out of the pool for it.

sections.heading: REC — recovery, blast radius and quarantine
sections.body:
Thirteen requirements. The refusal contract — a rung whose blast radius exceeds what a live lease permits is refused and recorded, never quietly downgraded — is the part of this system most worth keeping, and it is implemented correctly.

What is missing is everything downstream of it: two of nine rungs cannot execute, refusals from one path are not queryable as refusals, and the operator action most likely to be taken before physical work — draining a host — writes a column the allocator has never read.

rows: Tiers are stored, not hard-coded, each with a blast radius and the minimum lease disruption policy it requires.
`farm.recovery_tiers`. The ladder table on this page renders from it, so a new rung appears without an edit.
A rung whose blast radius exceeds what a live lease permits is refused and recorded, never quietly downgraded.

`internal/recovery` reads `farm.leases` in exactly one function, only to decide whether it may act, and writes none. On this demo the per-device path has never run: of 48 refusal rows, 37 came from the simulator, 11 from the API, 0 from the ladder. `gap:recovery.17`
Tiers 3 (USBDEVFS_RESET) and 4 (VBUS power) execute against real hardware.

`farmd node` serves the two routes and nothing in the tree is an HTTP client for them; `cmd/farmd/roles.go:206` constructs `NewADBActuator(log, nil)` for `recovery`, `all` and `demo` alike. A device a USB reset would have fixed reaches quarantine two rungs early. `gap:recovery.1`
A rung that cannot run is refused with a reason naming what is missing, rather than reported as ineffective.
The right call, and it is made. Reporting `no_change` for a rung never attempted would quarantine a device whose real problem is that nobody is listening on the host.
A refusal is queryable as a refusal.

`Ladder.perform`'s switch passes through recovered/no_change/failed and maps everything else to `OutcomeFailed`, putting the text in `detail.refusal`. So `WHERE outcome='refused'` — the obvious query, and the one the dashboard uses — misses every missing-host-agent refusal.
Several devices failing together on one hub is ONE incident, not N.

`farm.v_fleet` joins quarantines on `device_id`, NULL for hub- and host-scoped rows, so the grid shows a quarantined device with no explanation. And the view's `unhealthy` is a different definition from the ladder's, so the banner and the quarantine reason report different counts on the same hub. `gap:recovery.7`, `gap:recovery.8`
Draining a host stops new leases landing on it.

`POST /hosts/{id}/drain` sets `admin_state='draining'` and returns `no new leases will be placed on this host`. `farm.lease_acquire` never reads it. Verified live: h02 was drained and seven new leases were acquired on it in the next sixty seconds.
Closing a quarantine returns its devices to the pool.

The close updates `farm.quarantines`; the health write that makes devices schedulable lives in the ladder. With the recovery role down an operator can close every quarantine in the fleet, get 200 every time, and no device comes back. It also never restores `farm.devices.admin_state`.
Quarantine can be scoped to the granularity of the actual fault.

`scope` permits `slot` and `power_domain` and there is a partial unique index for `slot`; no code writes either, and there is no `power_domain_id` column, so a power-domain quarantine cannot name its subject. On mixed hardware the choice is one device or the whole hub.
The ladder's first action on a settled unhealthy device is the cheapest rung.

Tier 0 is unreachable: `ladder_tier` defaults to 0 and `next()` returns the first rung with `tier > cur`. The debounce still happens, from a different mechanism — but the table advertises a rung that never runs and a budget never spent.
An action recorded as an open recovery attempt is closed by whoever performs it.

`POST /slots/{id}/power` writes a tier-4 row and promises the host agent will close it. No code anywhere reads `farm.recovery_attempts`. Verified: three rows open at NULL outcome, oldest 28 minutes, each holding an hourly budget slot. A 202 means recorded, not switched.
Bulk selection does not sweep up devices that are quarantined or unhealthy.

`expandBulkSelector` filters on devpath, endpoint and `admin_state='enabled'` only. Verified: a run against h02 hit all seven devices of a quarantined hub and five errored. Harmless for a `getprop`; a `reboot` across it produces a wave of failures.
Recovery history is queryable by the questions an operator actually asks.

`GET /api/v1/recovery` takes `device`, `host` and `limit`. `Show me every refusal at tier 4 in the last hour` cannot be asked. The `refusal` column exists so the UI can explain a gap; the endpoint does not let you find the gap.

examples.label: REC-07 and JOB-11: what the allocator does not read
examples.code:
grep -c selector migrations/00002_lease.sql
grep -n 'farm\.hosts' migrations/00002_lease.sql
grep -n admin_state migrations/00002_lease.sql
examples.output:
0
79:  EXECUTE 'GRANT SELECT ON farm.devices, farm.slots, farm.hosts TO farm_watchdog';
239:       AND d.admin_state = 'enabled'
262:        AND d.admin_state = 'enabled'
examples.note: The file that defines `farm.lease_acquire` mentions `selector` zero times, mentions `farm.hosts` once and only in a GRANT, and checks `admin_state` twice — both times on `d`, the **device**, never on `h`, the host. So a drained host still receives leases and a selector never narrows placement. Two API surfaces describe behaviour this file does not contain.

sections.heading: API — the HTTP surface, the CLI and artifacts
sections.body:
Nine requirements. The envelope and the status-code discipline are right, and `API-01` matters more than it looks: conflating 410 fenced with 503 transient is STF #663 reached through a different door.

`API-03` is the one with deployment consequences. The artifact path works only because the runner and the API share a disk, so it does not survive the split-role deployment the compose file's own `farm` profile describes.

rows: Every non-2xx body is one envelope, and 410 fenced (abort) is distinguishable from 503 transient (lease untouched).
The distinction is carried all the way into `internal/lease`. Conflating the two is #663 with a different trigger.
The role an endpoint needs is chosen at registration, not inside the handler, so no endpoint can exist without a level.

`buildHandler` wraps every route in `tenant(...)` or `operator(...)` **except one**: `GET /api/v1/capabilities` is registered with a bare `mux.HandleFunc` at `router.go:55`. The exception is deliberate and reasoned — an operator debugging a farm whose auth is the broken thing still needs to see its state — but it is not what the invariant says, and it is what `SEC-08` costs. Under `AllowAll` the split never decides anything anyway; see `SEC-01`.
The reference recovers from a transient fetch failure.

`ensureArea` caches `{error: …}` on failure and its own guard `if (cache.has(area) …) return` then blocks every retry for the life of the page; `ensureMeta` latches the same way on `metaErr`. One dropped request — on the flaky link this product is otherwise designed for — makes an area unreadable until a full reload, with no retry affordance and a card that looks like it is still working.
An artifact's bytes are fetchable over HTTP, so roles can be split across hosts.

Five metadata routes are mounted; `Store.Get` and `Backend.Open` have no HTTP caller and the `url` field is a `file:///…` path on the API host's own disk. The runner works only because it is the same process tree on the same disk.
Disk under the artifact directory is reclaimable.

DELETE removes the row and retains the bytes by design; `artifacts.Backend` has no removal verb and no sweeper ships. Verified: blobs on disk with no matching row. Reclaiming space is a manual `find`, and nothing tells you when or how much.
A method mismatch returns 405 with an `Allow` header.

`mux.Handle("/api/v1/", …)` matches everything under the prefix, so Go's method-mismatch handling never fires and both directions return `404 not_found`. A client that special-cases 405 retries a method error as a missing resource.
`ctl` exit codes distinguish `the control plane failed` from `a target failed`.

`ctl bulk` returns 1 when a run completed with any target error. 6 ok, 1 transport error, run state `done` exits 1 — so a script treating 1 as a control-plane failure pages on a single offline handset.
`ctl` validates against the server, which is the authority.

No `ctl` code references `specs/validate`, `specs/kinds` or `specs/resets`; both `validate` and `submit` run `jobspec.Parse` locally. The comment beside that call says the server is the authority and is wrong on both counts.
`notImplemented()` has no callers, so exit 3 is unreachable. Harmless, except that it also strands `config.Summary()`, whose only call site it is — see `OBS-06`.

sections.heading: SEC — authentication, authorisation and the fence at the resource
sections.body:
Eight requirements, none met. That is expected — the README says authentication is a stub and the fence proxy is unbuilt — but three of these rows are worse than an absence, because the product tells operators otherwise.

`SEC-02`: the capability panel at the top of this page prints a fix (`set FARM_API_TOKENS`) for a variable with no consumer. `SEC-04`: the revoke response body and `ctl lease revoke` both say the previous holder's socket is `refused at the host proxy`, and no host proxy exists. `SEC-05`: a tenant check is deliberately skipped on renew because a code comment asserts that `holder_instance` never leaves the acquirer, and a farm-wide GET returns it.

A wrong remedy is worse than a documented absence: it converts an open port into an open port somebody believes they closed.

`SEC-08` is the row that survives fixing the others. `GET /api/v1/capabilities` is the single route in `buildHandler` registered with no role, for a defensible reason — an operator debugging a farm whose auth is the broken thing still needs to see its state. The consequence is that in a deployment where tokens finally work, that one route still hands an anonymous caller the fleet inventory counts, the lease timings and the per-role liveness of the whole farm.

rows: Callers are authenticated, and the operator role is not handed to everyone.

`cmd/farmd/roles.go:148` appends `AllowAll` unconditionally. Verified: 200 with no header and 200 with a fabricated bearer token, on operator-only routes. Anyone who reaches the port can revoke leases, drain hosts, power-cycle slots and delete artifacts.
The remedy the system prints for `SEC-01` works.
`api.AuthenticatorFromEnv` — which reads `FARM_API_TOKENS` and returns a constant-time bearer authenticator — has zero callers. The capability panel reports the fix anyway.
The audit trail records who, not only what.
Every `farm.audit_log` row written through the API carries actor `anonymous`, including operator `reason` text on revokes and drains. The trail is complete and anonymous.
A fenced holder cannot reach the device.

No Go file reads `devices.fence_floor` to gate an ADB operation, and `FARM_NODE_SELF_FENCE_TIMEOUT` has no consumer. The real barrier after a revoke is the 35s slot rearm — and the old holder may not notice for a full 60s renewal interval, which is longer. Size the rearm accordingly.
The secret half of the renew triple does not leak.

Renew skips a tenant check **because** a comment asserts `holder_instance` is never exposed by a farm-wide view. `GET /api/v1/leases` returns it for every lease, so `lease_id`, `fence` and `holder_instance` are readable from one unauthenticated GET.
A job id is not sufficient to take a live lease away from its holder.

`lease_acquire` is idempotent on `job_id` and its re-attach path overwrites `holder` and `holder_instance`. The previous holder's next renew returns 410 at an **unchanged** fence — indistinguishable from a release. Job ids are readable from three surfaces.

`tenantScope` is applied in eight places; `/events`, `/fleet`, `/topology`, `/hosts`, `/recovery`, `/bulk` and `/stream` are not among them. The stream is hardest: one shared poller fans out one shared snapshot, so scoping it means a poller per tenant.
Wiring a token closes every route that carries fleet state.

`GET /api/v1/capabilities` is the one route registered with no role (`API-02`), so it stays open even in the deployment where `SEC-01` and `SEC-02` are fixed. It returns device, host, live-lease, quarantine, job and artifact counts, the VCS revision, the schema version, the lease TTL/grace/renew/rearm and reaper gap-floor timings, per-role liveness — and, while auth is open, a sentence stating that anyone reaching the port can revoke leases and power-cycle slots. Serve the auth-and-build half unauthenticated and put the fleet counts behind the tenant role.

examples.label: SEC-01 and SEC-02: what is wired, and what is not
examples.code:
grep -rn WithAuthenticator cmd/farmd/
grep -rn AuthenticatorFromEnv --include=*.go . | grep -v internal/api/auth.go
examples.note: One unconditional `AllowAll`, and zero references to the function that would read `FARM_API_TOKENS`. The variable is not merely unwired — it is named as the fix in `authInfo()`, so the panel above tells an operator to do something that has no effect. Deleting that fix string is a smaller change than wiring the authenticator and is the more urgent of the two.

sections.heading: OBS — observability
sections.body:
Ten requirements, one met. The one that is met is the one that matters most: `obs.Register` pre-creates the children of the two series that mean `work was destroyed`, because a counter with no observations has no series and `increase(x[15m]) > 0` over a series that does not exist never fires.

`OBS-09` and `OBS-10` are about the panel at the top of this page rather than about Prometheus, and they compound: the panel discards the error from every one of its three database probes and returns 200 anyway, so a farm whose database is unreachable is described here as a farm with an empty schema, no devices and no roles beating — nine specific untrue statements, none of them flagged.

`OBS-03` is the row to read before touching any of this. Nine packages define `Collectors()` and one is registered, which reads like a one-line fix — and it is not. `internal/obs` and `internal/recovery` both produce a metric named `farm_recovery_attempts_total`, with different label sets. Prometheus refuses the second registration and `newRegistry` propagates the error, so adding `recovery.Collectors()` makes `farmd` **fail to start**. The rename comes first, or the fix looks like a regression.

rows: The two series that mean `work was destroyed` are armed from the first scrape of a fresh process, not from the first casualty.
`obs.Register` pre-creates the `lease_reaped_total` and `lease_renew_failures_total` children. The one metrics requirement that is fully honoured.
Each role exports its own metrics.

Nine packages define `Collectors()`; one production call site exists and it registers `adbwire`'s. Dead: `farm_scheduler_leader` and `farm_reaper_leader`, whose sum across replicas must be exactly 1, and `farm_jobrunner_panics_total`, whose help text says to alert on any rate above zero.

`obs` declares namespace `farm` + name `recovery_attempts_total` with five labels; `recovery` declares namespace `farm` + subsystem `recovery` + name `attempts_total` with two. Both resolve to the same fully-qualified name. Registering the second fails, and the failure is fatal at startup.
The Go runtime and process collectors are exported.
`internal/obs` deliberately leaves this to the binary, and the binary does not do it. No goroutine count, no RSS, no GC.
`MetricsAddr` appears in `config.go` and in the summary string and nowhere else; `/metrics` is served on `FARM_API_ADDR`. The Dockerfile's `EXPOSE 9090` documents a port nothing listens on.
A running `farmd` can be asked what configuration it booted with.

`config.Summary()`'s only call site is inside `notImplemented()`, which has no callers. And reconstructing it from the environment does not work either, because four variables are validated and then ignored — see `LEASE-12`, `LEASE-09`, `OBS-05`, `OPS-09`.
A rising `refused_ganged` rate tells you the rack needs per-port power switching.
The only producer is the ladder's per-device path, which has never run here; the demo hardcodes `refused_policy` even for its own ganged refusals. Live `/metrics` carries three outcome values.
Alerting rules, runbooks and a pager path ship with the tree.

There is no `docs/`, no `deploy/`, no `.github/`. `Hold and page` is one WARN line plus two counters that are not exported. A protected lease that goes suspect is held indefinitely and correctly, and nobody is told.
The capability panel says so when it could not measure, instead of reporting the unmeasured value.

All three probes swallow their error — `schemaInfo` and `fleetCounts` discard it with `_ =`, `roleStatuses` fills its map only `if err == nil` — and `handleCapabilities` returns 200 regardless. With Postgres unreachable the page renders `schema v0`, the note `no migrations applied; run farmd migrate up`, every role `never beat`, zero devices, and `No reaper is beating: an abandoned lease will never be reclaimed`. All of it false, none of it flagged, and the 200 means the dashboard's own control-plane banner never fires either.
`FARM_MIGRATIONS_TABLE` is honoured by everything that reads the migration table.

`migrate` calls `goose.SetTableName(cfg.MigrationsTable)`; `schemaInfo` hardcodes `FROM goose_db_version`, unqualified, while the default is `public.goose_db_version`. An operator who sets the variable gets a failing query, and — because of `OBS-09` — is then told `schema v0, no migrations applied` about a fully migrated database.

grep -rln '^func Collectors' --include=*.go internal/
grep -rn '\.Collectors()' --include=*.go internal/ cmd/ | grep -v _test.go

internal/enroll/enroll.go
internal/jobrunner/jobrunner.go
internal/node/agent.go
internal/reaper/reaper.go
internal/recovery/ladder.go
internal/scheduler/scheduler.go
internal/topo/discover.go
internal/watchdog/watchdog.go

internal/api/server.go:369:		for _, c := range adbwire.Collectors() {
examples.note: Everything the scheduler, reaper, jobrunner, recovery, watchdog, topo, enroll and node measure is compiled and never scraped. An alert written against any of those names will never fire — including the one meant to page when discovery stops succeeding.

examples.label: OBS-03: why registering them breaks the binary
examples.note: `farm` + `recovery_attempts_total` and `farm` + `recovery` + `attempts_total` are the same fully-qualified name. The first carries `{tier,outcome,host,hub,rack_slot}`, the second `{tier,outcome}`. Prometheus rejects the second registration with `a previously registered descriptor with the same fully-qualified name … has different label names`, and `newRegistry` returns that error rather than swallowing it. Rename one, then register the rest.

sections.heading: TEST — what is actually proved
sections.body:
Six requirements. The SQL protocol is genuinely proved — and running those assertions against a real PostgreSQL 17.10 rather than reading the SQL found three defects that reading had not, including a `lease_witness` comparison that could never match any live lease.

The Go side is not proved at all. Seven test files exist in a twenty-package tree, and none of them is in a package that makes a lease decision.

rows: The lease protocol is proved against a real PostgreSQL.

`test/assertions.sql` — 15 assertions, all passing. Running them rather than reading them found `#variable_conflict` shadowing in two functions, a witness comparison that could never match, and a `SET LOCAL ROLE` that leaked into the caller's transaction.
The assertions run against the database you care about.

The fixture inserts `racks('r1')`, `hosts('h01')`, `pools('default')` and `tenants('acme')`, all of which the demo seed owns, so the suite aborts on a duplicate key before the first assertion. Verifying the protocol means a scratch database — which means not verifying the one you care about.
The most expensive failure mode has a regression test that is watching it.

P10 cannot construct the state it is meant to test: it cannot move `expires_at` backwards, so both functions match zero rows and it passes trivially. Deleting `AND l.protected = false` from `lease_reclaim` would not fail the suite.
The Go decision points are tested.

Seven `_test.go` files, in `internal/adbwire` (4), `internal/jobspec` (2) and `test/fakeadb` (1). Sixteen packages report `[no test files]`, including `lease`, `reaper`, `scheduler`, `api`, `runner`, `jobrunner` and `recovery`. Two of the SQL defects in `DEV-02` would each have been caught by one test.
The suite runs on every change.
There is no `.github` directory. Nothing runs `go test`, `gofmt` or the assertions automatically.
Documentation claims are executed before they ship.

304 examples run against a live farm, 108 wrong and fixed, 98 claims corrected against the files they cite. A third of documentation written from reading code did not survive being run — which is why every row above cites a command rather than a conclusion.

examples.label: TEST-04: the whole test suite
examples.output:
internal/adbwire/client_test.go
internal/adbwire/device_test.go
internal/adbwire/errors_test.go
internal/adbwire/sync_test.go
internal/jobspec/pointer_test.go
internal/jobspec/spec_test.go
test/fakeadb/server_test.go
examples.note: The `ErrFenced`-versus-transient branch in `holder.go` — the branch whose own doc comment calls it the single most consequential decision in this project — is in none of these. A regression in it, or in `isRetryable` or `planResume`, would ship silently, and any of the three reintroduces #663.

sections.heading: OPS — deployment and operability
sections.body:
Ten requirements. The packaging is good and deliberately opinionated: no default role, so a manifest with a typo fails instead of starting something plausible; migrations embedded and refusing to be empty, because goose asked for zero migrations applies zero, reports success and exits 0.

`OPS-04` is the highest-leverage row in the entire register. `farmd node` cannot start in any environment, and it is the sole blocker under `DEV-04`, `DEV-05`, `REC-03` and `HW-06`. The cause is a guard and a default that contradict each other: `node.New` errors when `Addr` is set and `Token` is not, and `FARM_NODE_ADDR` cannot be blanked because the loader treats an empty value as unset and substitutes `:8082`.

rows: One static binary; every role is a subcommand, so a reaper cannot run a different commit than the scheduler it races with.
Distroless, `CGO_ENABLED=0`, no shell, no package manager, and **no default role**.
Migrations travel inside the binary and run from any working directory.

A `//go:embed` pattern matching no files is a build error, and an init-time check catches `at least one file` not being `the schema` — because an empty migration set is the quiet failure: zero applied, success reported, exit 0.
The system is runnable with no hardware, against the real control plane.

56 simulated devices across 2 in-process fake ADB servers driving the real scheduler, lease store, reaper, ladder and runner. The fake is only the hardware. `scripts/dev-up.ps1` stands up a throwaway PostgreSQL on a private port and never touches an existing service.

`runNode` passes `Addr` and never `Token`; `node.New` errors whenever `Addr != "" && Token == ""`; and `FARM_NODE_ADDR` cannot be blanked. **There is no environment that satisfies the guard.** The cheapest fix in the register and the one that unblocks the most.
Each host agent is distinguishable in the heartbeat table.

`runNode` hardcodes `Component: "node"`, discarding the package's own `node:<host id>` default. In a multi-host fleet every agent writes the same row, so one healthy host's beat hides a dead host — exactly what the per-host key exists to prevent.
`docker compose --profile farm up -d` starts a real farm.

The `demo` service has no `profiles:` key, so the documented command also starts simulated hardware writing into the same database — and the second of `demo` and `api` to start fails to bind 8420. `--scale demo=0` works; `docker compose --profile farm config` shows it without a daemon.
Kubernetes manifests or a Helm chart ship.

The README's architecture diagram puts the control plane in Kubernetes and nothing in the repo will put it there. The operator also writes their own answers to singleton replica counts, PodDisruptionBudgets that respect the advisory-lock leaders, and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` exceeding `FARM_SHUTDOWN_GRACE`.
SIGTERM drains work and releases nothing.
Deliberate. A shutdown that released leases would be the same failure as a socket error releasing them.
`FARM_COMPONENT` and `FARM_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` are honoured by the roles that read them.

`FARM_COMPONENT` is honoured by `api` only; every other role hardcodes its name, so a name set to satisfy the preflight never reaches `farm.component_heartbeat` and buys nothing in `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS`. `FARM_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` affects only roles that serve HTTP.
A default profile exists, so a reset tier has meaning on a fresh farm.
Without it `GET /api/v1/specs/resets` could only answer 404, because `medium` is defined as uninstall everything the profile does not own. This makes the tier definable, not effective — see `JOB-06`.

sections.heading: HW — the physical farm, its suppliers and its hazards
sections.body:
Seven requirements that do not live in the code, and two of them are the reason the code exists at all. They are recorded here because an operator who rediscovers them during procurement — or during an incident — rediscovers them at the worst possible moment.

`HW-01` is why this is a hardware project rather than an integration. Managed device clouds do not decline this workload on price or capability; four of them exclude it in writing. Renting is not an option that was evaluated and rejected. For continuous unattended use of third-party apps, it is an option that does not exist.

`HW-03` is the row most likely to be got wrong by someone acting in good faith. The instinct on being told `a rack of lithium cells` is to buy a clean-agent bottle. The measured result is that it does not work: in the Fire Safety Journal work, Novec 1230 at 8.5 vol% failed both to suppress the fire and to prevent propagation to neighbouring cells — and propagation occurred even in a pure-nitrogen atmosphere, because thermal runaway supplies its own oxidiser. Removing the oxygen does not stop it. What works is physical and procedural: containment, cell-to-cell spacing, charge limiting, and early detection. The product supports none of them, and `DEV-09` is why that is a shorter fix than it sounds.

rows: Continuous, unattended, long-running use of third-party apps on managed device clouds.

Four suppliers, four clauses. Sauce Labs restricts use to `legitimate testing or validation` in its AUP, and ToS §1.1 makes the AUP a licence condition. AWS Service Terms §35.2 forbids rooting or unlocking and forbids installing `persistent software on devices`. BrowserStack §4.3 requires the customer to warrant rights over `the application package itself`. Kobiton §2.3 forbids re-providing device access.
~50–60 handsets across a small number of bare-metal hosts.

28 per host is STF's own reference build: four powered seven-port hubs on a dedicated PCIe USB 3.0 card. Two hosts for 50–60; three if you want to drain one for maintenance — which today is a physical drain, because the software one does not work (`REC-07`).
Fire mitigation appropriate to a rack of lithium cells.

Clean-agent suppression does not stop a lithium event: Novec 1230 at 8.5 vol% failed to suppress **and** failed to prevent propagation, which occurred even in pure nitrogen. The mitigations that work are containment, spacing, charge limiting and early detection. The product collects neither charge nor temperature — see `DEV-09`.
Compliance with the fire code's energy-storage threshold.

IFC Table 1207.1.1 sets the lithium-ion ESS threshold at 20 kWh. A phone battery is roughly 17 Wh, so ~60 handsets is on the order of 1 kWh — about 5% of the trigger. The code is not what stops you; **operator and landlord policy is**, and that is a conversation to have before the hardware arrives. This row does not make `HW-03` smaller.
Per-port USB power switching, so tier 4 can cycle one port.

The schema models `per_port` and `ganged` and the ladder respects the difference. Two things blunt it: the demo seed gives even `per_port` hubs a single domain (`DEV-06`), and the `acknowledged` field that would let the control plane tell the agent every lease in the domain permits it is never populated — so on ganged hardware the agent refuses tier 4 unconditionally. `gap:recovery.11`
Linux 6.0 or newer on every host.

Below 6.0 the kernel silently re-powers a disabled port, so a cycle that appears to succeed did nothing — worse than a refusal, because it teaches the ladder to escalate past a rung that never ran. Nothing in `internal/node` or `internal/topo` has run against a phone, and bring-up cannot begin until `OPS-04` is fixed.
A PostgreSQL version the schema actually runs on is stated somewhere.

`docker-compose.yml` pins `postgres:17-alpine` and nothing declares a version requirement — while `farm.resolve_device` rung 2 needs a `min(uuid)` aggregate PostgreSQL 17 does not have. The error handler even logs `check the PostgreSQL version against migrations/00004_operate.sql`, so the failure was anticipated and never gated.

sections.source: README.md, migrations/00001_core.sql, migrations/00004_operate.sql, external supplier terms and fire-test literature

sections.heading: Reconciling the capability panel above with this register
sections.body:
`internal/api/capabilities.go` hand-maintains a twelve-entry feature list, rendered at the top of this page as **What is enabled, and how**. Six entries compute their state from a heartbeat; six are hardcoded. It is the most-read status surface in the product, so where it disagrees with the register, that is a defect in the list rather than a difference of opinion.

The two entries worth fixing first are `Automatic reclamation`, whose detail claims to be the only automatic release path when `lease_expire_max_runtime` is a second one that none of the reaper's controls reach; and `Recovery ladder`, whose detail branches on whether a `node` role is beating when the thing that actually decides is whether a `HostRunner` was wired — and it never is. A beating node agent would make that sentence appear, and it would still be false.

Three further defects are not about any single entry, but about the panel itself. It is registered without a role, so it is the one surface a token does not close (`SEC-08`). It discards the error from all three of its database probes and answers 200 regardless, so an unreachable database renders here as a confident diagnosis (`OBS-09`). And it reads `goose_db_version` directly rather than `cfg.MigrationsTable`, so an operator who set `FARM_MIGRATIONS_TABLE` is told their fully migrated database has no schema (`OBS-10`).

rows: Understates the risk. Jobs execute; they are not validated first, so `enabled` covers a path that allocates a real device to an unrunnable spec.
`the only automatic release path in the system`

**Wrong.** `farm.lease_expire_max_runtime` is a second automatic path, gated by neither `reaper_state.enabled` nor `quiesce_until` — so this entry reads `unavailable` while leases are still being ended.
True in production, misleading here: on the demo the simulator is a second writer with different rules.
**Wrong predicate.** The actuator's `HostRunner` is nil unconditionally at `cmd/farmd/roles.go:206`. Key the detail on the wiring, not the heartbeat.
Right answer, incomplete reason. It is not that no enroller is beating; it is that none **can** beat — see `OPS-04`.
Overstates. No enumeration, no mkdir, sizes truncated above 4 GiB — and push, install and pull have never completed on this deployment.
Overstates. Content addressing and the `EnsureOnDevice` skip work; there is no way to fetch bytes over HTTP and no way to reclaim disk.
True. Unscoped, which the entry does not say.
State agrees. The **fix string is wrong**: `authInfo()` names `FARM_API_TOKENS`, which has no consumer.
Agrees, and is the most honest entry in the list — while the revoke response body a few routes away says the opposite.

Five things an operator would reasonably assume exist are not in the list at all: host drain, reset tiers, selector placement, witness extensions, per-role metrics. A feature list that names only built features cannot warn you about the ones you assumed.

sections.heading: Where the requirements came from
sections.body: Nine commits, six area pages and three external findings. The column worth reading is the last one: in five of the nine commits the notable thing is a defect found by **running** the code rather than by reading it, and in three of those the defect would have destroyed a healthy device or a healthy job.

rows: The founding commit. Fixes three blockers a design critique flagged; all three still hold.
Three defects found by running the SQL against PostgreSQL 17.10 rather than reading it, including a witness comparison no live lease could ever match.
Tiers stored rather than hard-coded; quarantine scoped so six devices on one hub is one incident.
The import-barrier test caught a comment this commit's own author wrote, which is the point of it.
A serial alone identifies nothing. The clone flag is only computable after the insert, because the second clone's own lookup still counts one.
Hardening caught `pm clear` failing on a package that is not installed — every first reset of every newly enrolled device would have quarantined a healthy phone for being clean.
Four defects found by running it: no file transfer at all, a decorative per-transfer context, pointer payloads skipping every validation rule, and `Kind()` panicking on a typed nil.
No default role, so a manifest with a typo fails instead of starting something plausible.
`TEST-06`, and the 88 gap entries behind most rows above
304 examples executed, 108 wrong, 98 claims corrected. The ratio is the argument for the method.
Four suppliers, four separate clauses. The finding that makes this a hardware project.
Novec 1230 at 8.5 vol% failed to suppress and failed to prevent propagation; propagation occurred in pure nitrogen.
IFC Table 1207.1.1: 20 kWh. ~60 handsets is about 1 kWh.

sections.heading: What the register argues for next
sections.body: Ordered by unblocked-per-unit-of-work, not by severity. Two of the first three are call sites for functions that are already written, documented and tested by inspection — which is what a register is for: it makes visible that the expensive work was done and the cheap work was not.
bullets: **1. `OPS-04` — make `farmd node` startable.** One guard and one default. It is the sole blocker under `DEV-04`, `DEV-05`, `REC-03` and `HW-06`, and nothing else in the register unblocks four rows.
**2. `JOB-05` — call `specSubmissionError`.** Written, documented as the gate, never called. One call site stops real devices being allocated to specs that cannot run.

**3. `SEC-02` — call `AuthenticatorFromEnv`, or delete the fix string.** The second half is a one-line change and is the more urgent of the two: a wrong remedy is worse than a documented absence, because it converts an open port into an open port somebody believes they closed.
**4. `REC-07` — teach `lease_acquire` about `hosts.admin_state`.** One predicate. The endpoint already exists and already promises it.
**5. `OBS-03` then `OBS-02` — rename the colliding metric, then register the collectors.** In that order, or `farmd` fails to start and the fix looks like a regression.
**6. `JOB-06`/`JOB-07` — write `profile_id` and its three siblings from the API.** Until then every reset between tenants is a green step that cleans nothing.

**7. `DEV-09` — collect battery telemetry.** The column, the view, the API field and the CLI column all exist. This is the only row where a physical safety mitigation (`HW-03`) is waiting on a `dumpsys` call.

**8. `DEV-02`/`HW-07` — fix the `min(uuid)` rung and declare a PostgreSQL floor.** Sequence this **with** `OPS-04`: enrollment starting and then parking every new device at `pending` is a worse failure than enrollment not starting.
**9. `TEST-04`/`TEST-05` — a test for `isRetryable` and `planResume`, and something that runs it.** A regression in either reintroduces #663, which is the failure this project defines itself against.

gaps.what: `OPS-04`: `farmd node` cannot start in any environment. `runNode` passes `Addr: cfg.NodeAddr` and never passes `Token`, `node.New` errors whenever `Addr != "" && Token == ""`, and `FARM_NODE_ADDR` cannot be blanked because the config loader treats an empty value as unset and substitutes the `:8082` default.
gaps.consequence: This single guard is why four other rows in the register read `not_built`: `DEV-04` (dynamic enrollment), `DEV-05` (topology discovery), `REC-03` (recovery tiers 3 and 4) and `HW-06` (hardware bring-up). Nothing else in the register unblocks four requirements. It is also the reason the enrollment and topology machinery — several thousand lines of it, verified only by calling its SQL and its Go functions in isolation — has never run as a loop anywhere.

gaps.what: `JOB-05`: the spec gate is written and never called. `specSubmissionError` is documented at `internal/api/specs.go:565` as "the gate POST /api/v1/jobs applies to a spec" and `grep -rn specSubmissionError` returns its comment and its definition, nothing else.
gaps.consequence: A job whose spec cannot run is filed, the scheduler allocates a real device through `farm.lease_acquire`, and the runner discovers at `jobspec.Parse` that the document is nonsense. Verified live: seven jobs failed with `jobspec: invalid spec`, each having burned an attempt on a **different** device. Bad specs are never re-queued, so each one costs a phone and is permanent.

gaps.what: `SEC-02`: the remedy the product prints for its own open port does not work. `authInfo()` reports the fix as "set FARM_API_TOKENS to a token list"; `api.AuthenticatorFromEnv`, the only function that reads that variable, has zero callers anywhere in the tree.
gaps.consequence: An operator who reads the capability panel above, sets the variable and restarts has changed nothing, and now believes the port is closed. That is strictly worse than the documented absence beside it. Deleting the fix string is a one-line change and is more urgent than wiring the authenticator, because it converts a false sense of safety back into a known one.

gaps.what: `SEC-04`: the fence is not enforced at the resource, and the product's own text says it is. The revoke response body and `ctl lease revoke` both print "any socket still carrying fence N is refused at the host proxy"; no host proxy exists, no Go file reads `devices.fence_floor` to gate an ADB operation, and `FARM_NODE_SELF_FENCE_TIMEOUT` has no consumer.
gaps.consequence: An operator who revokes a lease and reads the reply believes the previous holder was cut off at the wire. The real barrier is the 35-second slot rearm — and a wedged holder may not notice its own eviction for a full 60-second renewal interval, which is **longer** than the rearm. The capability panel above is honest about this; two other surfaces contradict it. Until the proxy exists, treat slot rearm as the barrier and size it against the renewal interval, not against the fence.

gaps.what: `REC-07`: host drain is written and never read. `POST /api/v1/hosts/{id}/drain` sets `farm.hosts.admin_state='draining'` and returns "no new leases will be placed on this host". `farm.hosts` occurs once in `migrations/00002_lease.sql`, inside a GRANT, and both `admin_state` checks in `lease_acquire` are on the device, not the host.
gaps.consequence: An operator drains a host before physical work and believes jobs have stopped landing on it. Verified live: h02 was drained and acquired seven new leases in the following sixty seconds while reading `draining` throughout. The only thing that actually stops allocation to a host is a host-scoped quarantine, because that writes a column the allocator reads. Physically unplugging a hub is currently more reliable than the drain endpoint.

gaps.what: `JOB-06`: reset tiers expand to nothing. `farm.jobs.profile_id` is never written by any code path — two hits in the tree, both reads — and the reset expansion needs a profile to know which packages a job did not install.
gaps.consequence: Every `reset` step above tier `none` expands to zero sub-steps, reports `state = ok`, and cleans nothing. Verified live: a `reset-soft` step at `state=ok` with `detail: {"tier":"soft","profile":"","sub_steps":0}`. An operator who sets a reset tier and watches for green steps between tenants is watching devices not be cleaned. This is the register's worst silent failure, because the signal it produces is the same colour as success.

gaps.what: `JOB-11`: `farm.jobs.selector` is stored, validated, echoed by the API and never used for placement. The string `selector` does not occur anywhere in `migrations/00002_lease.sql`, and `internal/lease/store.go` documents `ErrNoCapacity` as "no device … matched the job's selector", which is not what the SQL does.
gaps.consequence: A job asking for `{"model":"Pixel 7"}` gets whatever device is next in the failure-score ordering. Verified: a job with `selector: {"model":"NoSuchPhone9000"}` was granted a device at HTTP 200 where a working selector would have returned 409. Only `pin_device` narrows placement, so any capability-targeted workload has to pin by device id and lose the pooling.

gaps.what: `LEASE-09`: nothing produces a witness. `farm.lease_witness`, `Store.Witness`, `Holder.Witness`, `FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_INTERVAL` and `FARM_LEASE_WITNESS_MAX_EXT` all exist; `Holder.Witness`'s only caller is inside `internal/lease`, there is no API route, and no on-device agent touches a marker file.
gaps.consequence: The extension meant to protect a job that has lost the control plane but is demonstrably alive on the device never fires. Across 1117 leases, `witness_at` is NULL on every one and `witness_extensions` has never exceeded 0. A long job that loses the control plane gets exactly TTL plus grace and nothing more — which is the scenario the witness was designed for and the one where its absence is least visible in advance.

gaps.what: `OBS-03`: registering the role collectors is not a one-line fix, and attempting it as one breaks the binary. `internal/obs` declares namespace `farm` + name `recovery_attempts_total` with `{tier,outcome,host,hub,rack_slot}`; `internal/recovery` declares namespace `farm` + subsystem `recovery` + name `attempts_total` with `{tier,outcome}`. Both resolve to `farm_recovery_attempts_total`.
gaps.consequence: Prometheus rejects the second registration with "a previously registered descriptor with the same fully-qualified name … has different label names", and `newRegistry` propagates the error rather than swallowing it — so adding `recovery.Collectors()` makes `farmd` fail to start. Anyone fixing `OBS-02` in the obvious order will see a startup failure and read it as a regression in their own change. Rename one descriptor first, then register the other eight packages' collectors.

gaps.what: `DEV-09`: battery state of charge, battery temperature and the charge gate are modelled everywhere and collected nowhere. `farm.device_runtime` has all three columns, `farm.v_fleet` exposes two, `internal/api/fleet.go` serialises them and `ctl` prints them. The only writer in the tree is `internal/demo/seed.go`, once, at seed time.
gaps.consequence: Every battery reading visible on this system is a seeded constant. More seriously, this is the collection layer that the two fire mitigations which actually work — charge limiting and early thermal detection — would both be built on. A rack of 60 lithium cells with a schema for charge and temperature and no writer for either has the appearance of monitoring and none of the substance.

gaps.what: `HW-03`: the product supports none of the lithium mitigations that are known to work. Clean-agent suppression is not one of them: Novec 1230 at 8.5 vol% failed both to suppress a cell fire and to prevent propagation to its neighbours, and propagation occurred even in a pure-nitrogen atmosphere, because thermal runaway supplies its own oxidiser.
gaps.consequence: The mitigations that work are containment, cell-to-cell spacing, charge limiting and early detection. The first two are rack design and are outside the software. The second two are `DEV-09`, which is unwritten. The failure mode this entry exists to prevent is buying a clean-agent bottle and considering the hazard handled — the measured result says it will neither put the fire out nor stop it spreading. Note also that fire code is not the gate here: `HW-04`.

gaps.what: `DEV-02` and `HW-07`: `farm.resolve_device` rung 2 calls `min()` on a `uuid` column and PostgreSQL 17 has no `min(uuid)` aggregate, while `docker-compose.yml` pins `postgres:17-alpine` and nothing anywhere declares a version requirement.
gaps.consequence: Any resolution reaching rung 2 with a non-NULL fingerprint raises SQLSTATE 42883, which `enroll.classifyResolveError` maps to `pending` — so a brand-new phone, which has no brand and therefore a computed fingerprint, is recorded as pending forever and never joins the fleet. This is latent today only because `OPS-04` stops enrollment running at all. Fix them in that order and the first symptom of the node agent finally starting is every new device parking at `pending`.

gaps.what: `TEST-04` and `TEST-05`: seven `_test.go` files exist in a twenty-package tree — four in `internal/adbwire`, two in `internal/jobspec`, one in `test/fakeadb` — and there is no `.github` directory, so nothing runs `go test`, `gofmt` or `test/assertions.sql` automatically.
gaps.consequence: The `ErrFenced`-versus-transient branch in `holder.go`, whose own doc comment calls it the single most consequential decision in this project, is untested; so are `isRetryable`, `planResume`, the checkpoint fencing and the ladder's refusal path. `leaseOps` and `runner.Conn` are both interfaces created specifically so a stub could drive those branches, and neither stub exists. A regression in any of them ships silently, and three of them reintroduce #663.

gaps.what: `OPS-07`: no Helm chart and no Kubernetes manifests. `docker-compose.yml` is the only deployment artifact in the repository, while the README's architecture diagram places the whole control plane in Kubernetes.
gaps.consequence: An operator writes their own Deployments and, with them, their own answers to the questions this code has opinions about: which roles must be singletons, PodDisruptionBudgets that respect the advisory-lock leaders, ordering the migrate Job ahead of everything else, and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` exceeding `FARM_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` so that `OPS-08`'s drain-and-release-nothing actually completes.

gaps.what: `LEASE-08`: `farm.lease_expire_max_runtime` is a second automatic ending that none of the reaper's controls reach. It bumps neither `fence_floor` nor `slots.rearm_at`, has no `protected` filter, and is gated by neither `reaper_state.enabled` nor `quiesce_until`.
gaps.consequence: A holder ended by the sweep is not fenced and its device is schedulable the same instant with no quarantine — verified, the ended holder's write at the same fence was accepted afterwards. Marking a job protected does not protect it from its own `max_runtime`, and turning the reaper off during an incident does not stop these endings. The capability panel's "the only automatic release path in the system" is describing `lease_reclaim` alone.

gaps.what: `LEASE-03`: the Postgres role firewall is correct DDL that no deployment assumes. `farm_reaper`, `farm_scheduler` and `farm_watchdog` are created `NOLOGIN` with the right grants; no Go code issues `SET ROLE`, there is no per-component DSN, and every process connects with one `DATABASE_URL` — as `farm`, which on the demo is a superuser.
gaps.consequence: The one place the firewall genuinely binds is inside `farm.lease_reclaim`, whose function-level `SET role = farm_reaper` drops superuser for that function's duration. Everywhere else the grants describe an intent nobody is running under: the watchdog process could write `farm.leases` because it is not running as `farm_watchdog`. What actually holds the health plane away from the lease plane is the Go import barrier — real, enforced by a test, and a compile-time property of this build rather than a database guarantee.

gaps.what: `OBS-09`: the capability panel at the top of this page cannot tell "I measured zero" from "I could not measure". `schemaInfo` and `fleetCounts` discard their query error with `_ =`, `roleStatuses` populates its map only `if err == nil`, and `handleCapabilities` returns 200 in every case.
gaps.consequence: With PostgreSQL unreachable — or the pool merely saturated, which the package doc warns about by name — this page renders a diagnosis rather than an outage: `schema v0` with the note "no migrations applied; run farmd migrate up", every control-plane role "never beat", every fleet count zero, and features reading "No reaper is beating: an abandoned lease will never be reclaimed and its device stays out of the pool." Nine specific false statements, none flagged. And because the response is 200, the dashboard's own "control plane is not answering" banner never fires either, so the most alarming screen in the product appears during the one incident where it is not the truth. An operator acting on it would go looking for a missing migration during a database outage.

gaps.what: `SEC-08`: `GET /api/v1/capabilities` is the one route in `buildHandler` registered with a bare `mux.HandleFunc` rather than through `tenant(...)` or `operator(...)`, so it carries no role — which is also why `API-02`, the invariant that no endpoint can exist without a level, reads `partial` rather than `met`.
gaps.consequence: The exception is deliberate and the reasoning in the comment is sound: an operator debugging a farm whose auth is the broken thing still needs to see its state. But the route returns rather more than that — device, host, live-lease, quarantine, job and artifact counts, the VCS revision, the schema version, the lease TTL, grace, renewal and rearm windows, the reaper gap floor, and per-role liveness. So it is the one surface that stays open in the deployment where `SEC-01` and `SEC-02` are finally fixed. Split it: the build, schema and auth halves answer unauthenticated; the fleet counts and timings go behind the tenant role.

gaps.what: The capability panel at the top of this page disagrees with the register in three places: `Automatic reclamation` claims to be the only automatic release path (`LEASE-08` says otherwise), `Recovery ladder` branches its detail on whether a `node` role is beating when the deciding fact is that `HostRunner` is nil at `cmd/farmd/roles.go:206`, and `Authentication` prints a fix that does nothing.
gaps.consequence: The panel is the most-read status surface in the product and is measured from the live deployment, which is exactly why a wrong entry carries further than a wrong sentence in prose. The `Recovery ladder` entry is the subtle one: it is correct today only because no node agent can beat, so fixing `OPS-04` would make it start printing "a host agent is present, so tiers 3 and 4 can act" while tiers 3 and 4 remain unreachable.

gaps.what: `DEV-05`: topology discovery and enrollment run only inside the `farmd node` role, and `topo.Sysfs` refuses on any GOOS but Linux. Nothing in this repository can enroll a device or register a slot on a Windows or macOS host.
gaps.consequence: The Linux restriction is correct and unavoidable — `/sys/bus/usb/devices`, `USBDEVFS_RESET` and per-port VBUS have no equivalent elsewhere. What is worth knowing is that on Linux it is still unreachable, because of `OPS-04`. So `farm.identity_observations` and `farm.slot_occupancy` are empty on every deployment, all 56 devices carry `hw_fingerprint IS NULL`, and everything documented about the identity ladder was verified by calling its SQL and its Go functions directly rather than by watching the loop run.

gaps.what: `JOB-04`: checkpoint and resume are implemented and have never executed. The demo has never exercised the resume path, `internal/runner` has no test files, and `runner.Conn` is documented as an interface specifically so `planResume` and `isRetryable` could be driven by a fake without a phone — the fake does not exist.
gaps.consequence: Resume is the feature that makes a six-hour job survive a pod eviction, which is one of the two reasons the lease protocol was built the way it was. Its correctness currently rests on reading the code. Treat a resume in production as a first run: watch it, and expect the idempotent flag on `farm.step_kinds` to be the thing that decides whether a re-run repeats a side effect.

gaps.what: This register is a point-in-time verification and nothing re-checks it. Every status above was confirmed against this tree at the commit that added the file — by grep, by build, or against a live farm — and there is no test, no CI job and no assertion that fails when a row goes stale.
gaps.consequence: A row that reads `not_built` after somebody has built the thing is the same failure this page exists to prevent, pointed the other way. The cheapest guard is to treat the greps in the examples above as the register's test suite: each is a single command whose output is printed beside it, so a status is falsifiable in one paste. Until `TEST-05` exists there is nothing to hang them on.
